**It does not demand its own way:** Love is not self-centered, not concerned simply with its own interests (see [Phil 2:4-8](Phil.2.4-Phil.2.8)).
**Love***,* in contrast to spiritual gifts, **will last forever**.
**Love will last forever***,* because God is love (cp. [1 Jn 4:7-12](1John.4.7-1John.4.12), [16](1John.4.16)).
None of the spiritual gifts gives us full understanding; unlike love, they are all limited in their benefits.
The contrast between **now** and **then** is between this age and the coming age.

**Now we see things imperfectly, like puzzling reflections in a mirror:** In Paul’s day, mirrors were usually made of polished bronze, so the view was imperfect. Our perception in this life is limited and our understanding is **partial and incomplete**.
**then:** When the end comes and Christ establishes his eternal kingdom, **we will see everything with perfect clarity**. Then the spiritual gifts that give knowledge will be unnecessary.

**Faith, hope, and love** are more important than spiritual gifts because they **last forever** (see also [Rom 5:1-5](Rom.5.1-Rom.5.5); [Gal 5:5-6](Gal.5.5-Gal.5.6); [Col 1:4-5](Col.1.4-Col.1.5); [1 Thes 1:3](1Thess.1.3); [5:8](1Thess.5.8)). Of the three, **the greatest** . . . **is love***,* because love is the quintessential nature of God himself (see [1 Jn 4:7-12](1John.4.7-1John.4.12), [16-21](1John.4.16-1John.4.21)). So love should epitomize our relationship with him and others.

Having emphasized the supreme importance of **love** (ch [13](1Cor.13.1-1Cor.13.13)), Paul returns to the subject of spiritual gifts. Their relative value is defined by the benefit they give to others, which is characteristic of love (ch [13](1Cor.13.1-1Cor.13.13)). In that light, Paul contrasts the over-valued gift of tongues with the more beneficial gift of prophecy.

Of all **the special abilities the Spirit gives** (see study note on 12:1–14:40), Paul encourages the Corinthians to seek **the ability to prophesy** (see [12:10](1Cor.12.10)) because of its greater benefit to the church.

The problem with the gift of speaking **in tongues** is that hearers cannot readily **understand** the message; the gift of **prophecy***,* however, is immediately intelligible and beneficial as a word from God that **strengthens . . . encourages . . . and comforts** those who hear.
The primary purpose of spiritual gifts is not self-edification, but the strengthening of **the entire church** (see [12:7](1Cor.12.7); cp. [8:1](1Cor.8.1); [14:12](1Cor.14.12)).
A message needs to be clearly intelligible if it is to communicate effectively.
**Special abilities** from **the Spirit** are given to **strengthen the whole church** (see [12:7](1Cor.12.7); [14:4](1Cor.14.4); cp. [Eph 4:15-16](Eph.4.15-Eph.4.16)).
Paul does not forbid speaking in **tongues** (see [14:39](1Cor.14.39)), but **the ability to interpret** is crucial, especially in public worship (see [14:27-28](1Cor.14.27-1Cor.14.28)).
Speaking in tongues engages the **spirit** of the speaker (because the Holy Spirit is speaking through the person) but not his mind (because the message is not rationally intelligible).

It is preferable both to worship **in the spirit** and to use **words I understand** in worship and ministry because public worship should always bless both God and others. Speaking in tongues without interpretation, though it gives glory to God and edification to the speaker ([14:4](1Cor.14.4)), fails to benefit others who are present.
**praise God along with you** (literally *say “amen” to your thanksgiving*): *Amen* was the traditional congregational response to a prayer.
Paul affirmed the personal value of speaking **in tongues***,* but speaking **in a church meeting** should **help others***,* not only the speaker.
To **be mature in understanding** such **matters***,* one must consider the purpose of spiritual gifts and not treat them as ends in themselves for one’s own enjoyment.

Paul used this quotation from [Isa 28:11-12](Isa.28.11-Isa.28.12) to show that **speaking in tongues is a sign, not for believers, but for unbelievers**. However, in [1 Cor 14:23-25](1Cor.14.23-1Cor.14.25), Paul argues that even unbelievers are more likely to be convicted by a word of prophecy than by speaking in tongues. His point is that, in public worship, the gift of prophecy is of greater usefulness than the gift of tongues.
**“God is truly here among you.”** Paul is alluding to [Isa 45:14](Isa.45.14).

Paul gives specific procedures for the use of spiritual gifts in the church and emphasizes that they are to be expressed in an orderly way. Among the early Christians, **church meetings** were not led by professional pastors or priests. Instead, everyone shared with the others what God had given them for strengthening the church.
**will sing:** Literally *has a psalm*, either to be sung alone or for the fellowship to sing together (cp. [Eph 5:19](Eph.5.19); [Col 3:16](Col.3.16)).

**Everything that is done** in public worship is to be for the purpose of strengthening the church (see [1 Cor 12:7](1Cor.12.7); [14:4](1Cor.14.4), [6](1Cor.14.6), [12](1Cor.14.12), [26](1Cor.14.26); cp. [8:1](1Cor.8.1)).

For a church overly eager for the gift of **tongues** (see [12:10](1Cor.12.10)), Paul places limits on its public expression so it would be most helpful to the church: **no more than two or three,** . . . **one at a time***,* and only if there is someone present **who can interpret** the message.

Public **prophesying** is to be expressed in an orderly way, sensitive to the guidance of the Spirit, so that everyone may benefit from it. **The others** are then to **evaluate what is said** to assess whether it is indeed a word from God ([1 Thes 5:19-21](1Thess.5.19-1Thess.5.21)). Those with a word of prophecy are to **take turns**—prophecy is a divinely given word, but it is still subject to the **control** of the speaker.
This aside in the discussion on using spiritual gifts reflects a perspective on women’s roles similar to that of the Pastoral Letters (see [1 Tim 2:11-15](1Tim.2.11-1Tim.2.15)).

Paul advises women to **be silent** and **submissive** in church meetings. This instruction is to be understood in light of [1 Cor 11:5](1Cor.11.5), which clearly implies that women are permitted to pray and prophesy publicly.
**just as the law says:** Possibly referring to [Gen 3:16](Gen.3.16).
Paul expected the Corinthians to take his apostolic word seriously, as **a command from the Lord himself**.
**What I am saying** probably refers to all of his teaching, especially as it relates to spiritual gifts.
Paul summarizes his discussion of spiritual gifts (chs [12–14](1Cor.12.1-1Cor.14.40)).

Some people in the church had doubts about a future **resurrection of the dead**. Paul reassures them and, perhaps in response to their skeptical questions, discusses the nature of a resurrection body.
Paul summarizes the Good News that he preached.
At the heart of **the Good News** stands the message of the atoning death and resurrection of Christ (see [15:3-4](1Cor.15.3-1Cor.15.4); [Rom 5:8-10](Rom.5.8-Rom.5.10); [6:5-11](Rom.6.5-Rom.6.11)).

**if you continue to believe:** Those who continue firm in their faith will be saved (cp. [Matt 10:22](Matt.10.22); [24:13](Matt.24.13); [John 15:6](John.15.6); [Gal 5:4](Gal.5.4); [Col 1:23](Col.1.23); [Heb 6:4-6](Heb.6.4-Heb.6.6); contrast [1 Cor 1:8](1Cor.1.8); [Rom 8:38-39](Rom.8.38-Rom.8.39); [Phil 1:6](Phil.1.6); [Heb 6:9](Heb.6.9)).
The heart of the Good News is that **Christ died for our sins** (see [Rom 3:24-25](Rom.3.24-Rom.3.25); [5:8-10](Rom.5.8-Rom.5.10); [Gal 1:4](Gal.1.4); [1 Thes 5:9-10](1Thess.5.9-1Thess.5.10)).
**just as the Scriptures said:** See [Ps 16:10](Ps.16.10); [Hos 6:2](Hos.6.2); [Jon 1:17](Jonah.1.17); [Matt 12:40](Matt.12.40); [Acts 2:24-32](Acts.2.24-Acts.2.32).
**He was seen by Peter:** See [Luke 24:34](Luke.24.34).
**then by the Twelve:** See [Matt 28:16-17](Matt.28.16-Matt.28.17); [Mark 16:14](Mark.16.14); [Luke 24:36](Luke.24.36); [John 20:19](John.20.19).
**he was seen by more than 500:** We have no other account of this event.
**most of whom are still alive:** When this letter was written (around AD 53–56), the factuality of Christ’s resurrection could be verified by consulting living eyewitnesses.

This **James** was almost certainly Jesus’ brother, who became a leader of the Jerusalem church after Jesus’ death (see [Mark 6:3](Mark.6.3); [John 7:1-5](John.7.1-John.7.5); [Gal 1:19](Gal.1.19); cp. [Acts 12:17](Acts.12.17); [15:13](Acts.15.13); [21:18](Acts.21.18)).

**as though I had been born at the wrong time** (or *as though I were stillborn*): This phrase can refer to a miscarriage or stillbirth. Here it might express the unusual manner of Paul’s conversion, or the derogatory view some opponents held of his apostleship, or his own sense of unworthiness to be an apostle. The overall emphasis is on the extraordinary grace of God to Paul as a former persecutor of Christ’s people (see [Gal 1:13](Gal.1.13); [Phil 3:6](Phil.3.6); cp. [Acts 8:3](Acts.8.3); [9:1-2](Acts.9.1-Acts.9.2)).
**I also saw him:** Paul came face to face with the risen Christ at his conversion (see [1 Cor 9:1](1Cor.9.1); [Acts 9:3-6](Acts.9.3-Acts.9.6); [Gal 1:15-16](Gal.1.15-Gal.1.16)).

Paul’s awareness of God’s extraordinary **special favor** (literally *grace*) to him resulted in an extraordinary response on his part. But even that must be understood as an expression of **God . . . working through me by his grace** (see [2 Cor 4:7](2Cor.4.7); [Gal 2:20](Gal.2.20); [Col 1:27](Col.1.27)).
The important thing is the **message***,* not the messengers (cp. [1:10-12](1Cor.1.10-1Cor.1.12)).
Paul now makes the case for a future **resurrection**.
Christ’s resurrection confirms the reality of the future resurrection.

Some believers in Corinth apparently had a difficult time accepting the Jewish notion of a bodily **resurrection of the dead***,* preferring instead the Greek notion of the immortality of the soul (cp. [Acts 17:18](Acts.17.18), [32](Acts.17.32)).

If Christ has not risen from the dead, then Christian **faith is useless**. But in reality, Jesus’ resurrection is proof that the sacrifice of Christ fully atoned for human sins (see [15:3](1Cor.15.3)). **If Christ has not been raised***,* then human beings remain unforgiven, under the judgment of God—**still guilty of** their **sins** (see [Rom 3:19](Rom.3.19); [Eph 2:1-3](Eph.2.1-Eph.2.3)).

Without eternal life, faithful believers **are more to be pitied than anyone in the world** because they suffer persecution and deprivation. But they find their joy in anticipating what lies beyond this life, as did both Jesus (see [Heb 12:2](Heb.12.2)) and Paul (see [2 Cor 4:16-18](2Cor.4.16-2Cor.4.18); [Phil 1:21-23](Phil.1.21-Phil.1.23); [3:7-11](Phil.3.7-Phil.3.11)).

In the Old Testament, the first crop was dedicated to God (see [Exod 23:19](Exod.23.19)). Christ’s resurrection is **the first of a great harvest** of God’s people who will be resurrected (see [Col 1:18](Col.1.18)).
Adam’s sin contrasts with Christ’s resurrection (cp. [15:45-49](1Cor.15.45-1Cor.15.49)).
Christ is the Lord of all things, even **death** itself. Nevertheless, he remains subordinate to **God** his **Father**.

The phrase **every ruler and authority and power** refers to spiritual powers who oppose Christ (cp. [Rom 8:38](Rom.8.38); [Eph 1:21](Eph.1.21); [Col 2:10](Col.2.10), [15](Col.2.15); [1 Pet 3:22](1Pet.3.22)).
This paraphrase of [Ps 110:1](Ps.110.1) is applied to Jesus (cp. [Heb 1:13](Heb.1.13)).
**beneath his feet:** In the ancient Near East, victorious kings were depicted with their feet on the necks of their defeated enemies.
**“God has put all things under his authority”:** See [Ps 8:6](Ps.8.6); cp. [Matt 22:44](Matt.22.44).

Some first-century Christians apparently practiced baptism-by-proxy for dead unbelievers whom they wished to be saved. Paul neither endorses nor condemns the practice; he simply uses it as evidence for belief in resurrection. There is no other reference to such a practice in early Christian literature.
The apostles’ willingness to **risk** their **lives** was based on their conviction that there is life beyond death. If there is no resurrection, such suffering is pointless.

**fighting wild beasts—those people of Ephesus:** Paul refers figuratively to his struggles with opponents in Ephesus (see [16:8](1Cor.16.8); [Acts 19:23-41](Acts.19.23-Acts.19.41); [2 Cor 1:8](2Cor.1.8); [4:8-12](2Cor.4.8-2Cor.4.12); [11:23-28](2Cor.11.23-2Cor.11.28)). Watching condemned prisoners *fighting wild beasts* and getting mauled to death was a common form of entertainment in the Roman world.
**“bad company corrupts good character”:** This quotation from the Greek poet Menander (300s BC) is a warning not to listen to those who are teaching wrong things.
**some of you don’t know God at all:** Paul sharply rebukes those who prided themselves on their knowledge but remained skeptical of resurrection.

Paul discusses the nature of resurrection **bodies***,* perhaps responding to skeptical questions. In the Greco-Roman world, belief in the immortality of the soul was common, but not belief in the resurrection of the body.
**What a foolish question!** Paul’s strong response suggests that the question is skeptical. It might also imply that the answer is unknowable.

Just as the shape of a **plant** does not resemble the seed, yet the plant’s growth is determined by the kind of seed, so the resurrection body will be unlike the present body, yet identifiable as belonging to the same person.
Everything that God has made has its own **glory**—its own unique beauty and magnificence. The resurrection body will be unlike anything else.
Just as growing plants differ from the seeds out of which they sprout, so resurrection bodies will be vastly unlike our mortal bodies.

**Adam** and **Christ** founded two distinct humanities: One is natural and earthly, enslaved to sin and death; the other is spiritual and heavenly, purified and destined for life. Adam represents **the natural** (physical) **body** and Christ **the spiritual** (resurrection) **body**. See also [15:21-22](1Cor.15.21-1Cor.15.22); [Rom 5:12-21](Rom.5.12-Rom.5.21).
Just as Christ’s **life-giving Spirit** supersedes the natural life, the spiritual body will supersede the physical body.
**made from the dust of the earth:** Adam’s earthly origin ([Gen 2:7](Gen.2.7)) is here contrasted with Christ’s heavenly origin.
**Earthly people** (literally *those of the dust*): Like Adam, natural human beings are under the curse of sin and death. All return to dust (see [Gen 3:19](Gen.3.19))—they all die.
**heavenly people are like the heavenly man:** Those who belong to Christ are like him in having an unending spiritual life.

Like **the earthly man,** Adam, we have physical bodies in this life. But **we will someday be like** Christ, **the heavenly man***,* experiencing the Kingdom of God in resurrection bodies (cp. [Rom 6:4-14](Rom.6.4-Rom.6.14)).
**Physical bodies cannot inherit** God’s Kingdom. Only a spiritual, resurrected body can experience the Kingdom in all its fullness (cp. [John 4:24](John.4.24)).
The Good News reveals the previously unknown **secret** of resurrection.
**We will not all die:** Paul might have expected the future resurrection in his own lifetime (cp. [15:52](1Cor.15.52); [1 Thes 4:15](1Thess.4.15), [17](1Thess.4.17)).

**“Death is swallowed up in victory”:** Resurrection defeats the ultimate enemy, **death***,* just as the power of the Spirit enables believers to transcend sin here and now (see [Rom 8:2](Rom.8.2), [11](Rom.8.11)).
This quotation ([Hos 13:14](Hos.13.14)) assures believers that they have nothing to fear from **death**.
Death is like the **sting** of a scorpion.
The death and resurrection of Christ ends the dominating power of **sin** and **death** (see [Rom 6:14](Rom.6.14); [8:2](Rom.8.2); [10:4](Rom.10.4)).
**Nothing you do for the Lord is ever useless:** There will be eternal rewards for those who serve him faithfully (see [3:12-15](1Cor.3.12-1Cor.3.15)).

Paul answers the Corinthians’ **question** about the offering for poor Christians **in Jerusalem** ([Acts 24:17](Acts.24.17); [Rom 15:25-27](Rom.15.25-Rom.15.27); [2 Cor 8–9](2Cor.8.1-2Cor.9.15); [Gal 2:10](Gal.2.10)).
**Galatia** was a Roman province in Asia Minor (see [Acts 16:6](Acts.16.6); [18:23](Acts.18.23)).

Christians met **on the first day of each week** (see [Acts 20:7](Acts.20.7)) rather than the last day of the week, as in the Old Testament ([Exod 20:8](Exod.20.8); [34:21](Exod.34.21); [Isa 58:13-14](Isa.58.13-Isa.58.14)). The first day was the “Lord’s Day,” the day of the Lord’s resurrection ([Mark 16:9](Mark.16.9); [Luke 24:13-15](Luke.24.13-Luke.24.15); [John 20:19](John.20.19); [Rev 1:10](Rev.1.10)).

The **portion of the money you have earned** is not specified; Paul later encouraged them to give as generously as they could ([2 Cor 8:1-4](2Cor.8.1-2Cor.8.4); [9:6-13](2Cor.9.6-2Cor.9.13); cp. [Luke 12:33-34](Luke.12.33-Luke.12.34); [21:1-4](Luke.21.1-Luke.21.4); [1 Tim 6:18-19](1Tim.6.18-1Tim.6.19)).
Paul did in fact deliver the gift to Jerusalem ([Rom 15:25-26](Rom.15.25-Rom.15.26)).
Paul had traveled through **Macedonia,** a Roman province in the northern region of Greece, on his second missionary journey ([Acts 15:36–18:22](Acts.15.36-Acts.18.22)).
**planning to travel through Macedonia:** See [Acts 19:21](Acts.19.21); [20:1-3](Acts.20.1-Acts.20.3).
**possibly all winter:** Paul evidently made this visit (cp. [Acts 20:2-3](Acts.20.2-Acts.20.3)).
Paul wrote this letter while in **Ephesus** (about AD 53–56; [Acts 19:1–20:1](Acts.19.1-Acts.20.1)).
**Pentecost** was in May or June.
**When Timothy comes:** See [4:17](1Cor.4.17). Timothy was Paul’s child in the faith and co-worker (see [1 Tim 1:2](1Tim.1.2)).
**don’t intimidate him:** Timothy may have been shy ([2 Tim 1:6-8](2Tim.1.6-2Tim.1.8)).
**Apollos:** See study note on 1:12.
Together with **Stephanas** (see also [1:16](1Cor.1.16); [16:15](1Cor.16.15)), **Fortunatus** and **Achaicus** had apparently traveled from Corinth to visit Paul in Ephesus.
As in other letters, Paul greets his friends and gives a benediction.
**Aquila** and **Priscilla** (Greek *Prisca*) had previously moved from Corinth to Ephesus, where Paul was writing this letter (cp. [Acts 18:1-3](Acts.18.1-Acts.18.3)).
**gather in their home:** Aquila and Priscilla later continued this practice in Rome (see [Rom 16:3-5](Rom.16.3-Rom.16.5)).
**a sacred kiss:** A kiss on the cheek was a common greeting.

Paul takes up the pen and signs the letter in his **own handwriting**. As was common, Paul used a secretary to write this letter and others (see [Rom 16:22](Rom.16.22); [Gal 6:11](Gal.6.11); [Col 4:18](Col.4.18); [2 Thes 3:17](2Thess.3.17)).
To be **cursed** is to be condemned by God (see also [Rom 9:3](Rom.9.3); [Gal 1:8-9](Gal.1.8-Gal.1.9)).
**Our Lord, come!** This phrase was sometimes used in early Christian prayers (see also [Rev 22:20](Rev.22.20)).
All of Paul’s letters close with a benediction similar to this one.
Paul invokes **grace** at both the beginning and the end of this letter (see [1:3](1Cor.1.3)).
